title: Parallel Worlds: An Interview with Artist, Gaku Tsutaja
author: Rebecca Maria Goldschmidt
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-1-680x1010.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/05/parallel-
worlds-an-interview-with-artist-gaku-tsutaja/)

It makes sense that I would meet Gaku Tsutaja at a protest against the War on
Iran in front of Hiroshima’s Atomic Bomb Dome, the preserved relic of total
obliteration. It was June 2025 and the world was witnessing Israel’s surprise
attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities in the Twelve-Day War. Tsutaja was in
town for the exhibition opening of [_Between Memories and
Objects_](https://www.hiroshima-moca.jp/exhibition/memoriesandobjects?moca-
lang=en) at Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art. It seemed absurd to
think of art commemorating 80 years since the bomb while uranium enrichment
facilities were simultaneously being bombed in Iran… yet these are the
conditions of absurdity in which we live. Eight months later, as the 2026 War
on Iran escalated to new levels of violence and closer to nuclear disaster, we
worked through these interview questions, two artists meeting across time
zones, in the mess of the past and present.

Tsutaja’s work is, regrettably, more relevant than ever as the horrific
possibility of nuclear disaster hangs on every earthly moment. She excels at
synthesizing the twisted and torturous chapters of the American nuclear
program into metaphor, motif, and manga-style drawings, animations, and
sculptural installations. Her work covers some of the rawest and most
intentionally obscured aspects of American and Japanese Imperialism: [uranium
mining and its legacy on Congo](https://newrepublic.com/article/174374/first-
mined-atomic-bomb-now-theyre-mining-evs) and [American Indian
lands](https://haulno.com/); Unit 731 of Imperial Japanese Army and its human
medical experimentation; [Japanese-American
incarceration](https://densho.org/); the hydrogen bomb tests in the [Marshall
Islands](https://www.kathyjetnilkijiner.com/); Nishiyama Dam in Nagasaki
filled with the highest level of radiation black rain; Monsanto's plutonium
bomb detonators, Agent Orange, bovine growth hormone, white phosphorus
bombs…among many other human environmental atrocities.

Barely a century beyond these crimes, Japan’s crescendoing fascism is now
conducted by the first female prime minister, Takaichi, who insidiously
mirrors Trumpian policies on immigration, increased defense spending, and
closer ties with Israel. This “best friends” plotline with Japan as lapdog to
the Trump regime has been cultivated over years with Hiroshima as the
backdrop. From the [Obama-hibakusha hug](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-
pacific/shigeaki-mori-hiroshima-atomic-bomb-survivor-embraced-by-obama-
dies-88-2026-03-17/), to the [Hiroshima Peace Park and Pearl Harbor National
Memorial Sister Park
Agreement](https://japantoday.com/category/national/flame-from-hiroshima-a-
bombed-ruins-to-be-used-at-pearl-harbor-ceremony) (brokered by former U.S.
Ambassador to Japan, Rahm Emmanuel), Japan’s role as wartime enemy has been
officially relegated to the past. Tsutaja’s work holds a mirror up to this
fascist alliance, recalling the nightmares of past imperialist wars that seem
to be fading faster than ever.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-2.jpeg)

_Memory Bug: Blood Bed_ , 2023 Sumi ink and graphite on paper 14 x 11 inches
(35.6 x 27.9 cm). © Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Ulterior Gallery, New York

Her recent back-to-back exhibitions at the 80th anniversary exhibition of WWII
at the [Taro Okamoto Museum of Art](https://www.taromuseum.jp/), in Kawasaki,
Japan, and at [Ulterior
Gallery](http://www.ulteriorgallery.com/gaku_tsutaja_pidgingo_no_inko) in
Manhattan, brought her audience into an alternative land where parakeets in
lab coats conduct their studies and crank radios spew propaganda. Inside a
giant bamboo birdcage structure, viewers watch a video of _Pidgingo-no-Inko_ ,
featuring “Sisak,” a robot with a young boy’s voice, modeled after a prototype
of the [Norden bombsight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norden_bombsight)—the
world's first high-altitude aiming device, which was used for the atomic
bombings. He discusses the history of weapons development, targeting and
surveillance systems as weapons of "eyes," including the internet and AI.
Another masked character modeled after a Palestinian-American friend, speaks
about the political oppression he experienced as both an activist and a
citizen. Those two stories unfold simultaneously, while other voices chat and
mimic each other about wars and suffering, revealing methods and patterns of
empire and ruling class violence repeated and accumulating on a global scale
over time.

Viewers are invited to explore the cage, both inside and out, and to renew
their perception of it. Non-human figures—birds, insects, mammals, fish,
plants, objects, and weapons—are engaged as storytellers, their heads replaced
with other creatures or objects, their human bodies dressed as historical
figures. They are inhabitants of hypotheses that push the boundaries of the
unseen world, and narrators who question humanity.

Near the entrance of the cage hangs, _ONITAIJI: Fall_ , a painting depicting
the Press Code gag order put in place on Japan under the American General
Headquarters (GHQ) occupation after the war; the establishment and legacy of
the Atomic Bomb Casualty Commission (ABCC) that researched the Hibakusha and
conducted autopsies on 50,000+ bodies; and the anti-war movements that emerged
in Hiroshima at the outbreak of the Korean War.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-3-scaled.jpeg)

_Pidgingo-no-Inko_ , 2025, video 20 min, structure as a set, and _Risograph
Print_. Photo by Makoto Matsuno © Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Taro Okamoto
Museum of Art, Kawasaki and Ulterior Gallery, New York Onitaiji: Fall, 2024.
Acrylic on cotton canvas. 72 x 83 inches / 182.9 x 210.8 cm Private Collection
© Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Taro Okamoto Museum of Art, Kawasaki and Ulterior
Gallery, New York

I had a lot of questions for Tsutaja, who has spent hours listening to
testimonies of global _Hibakusha_ , visiting nuclear sites and archives. Most
recently, her work has made reference to the genocide in Gaza and the
occupation of Palestine. While working on a scene depicting anti-war activists
during the Korean War risking their lives to scatter anti-war leaflets,
evacuation warning leaflets issued by Israel began raining down over Gaza. The
censorship surrounding Hiroshima was originally the center of her painting
series, _Onitaiji_ , but she felt it necessary to include the events unfolding
in real time in Palestine.

“Having been aware of the history of propaganda and repression perpetrated by
both the Japanese and U.S. governments against _Hibakusha_ , I could
immediately recognize the absurdity of the U.S. government’s and mass media’s
coverage of the Palestinian issue,” she shared. But after referencing
Palestine in her work, Tsutaja began to experience her first layer of
censorship, when viewers complained about her political statements. “I hadn't
experienced that for the nuclear theme. Perhaps the taboo surrounding the
nuclear issue only applies to those involved in the military or government.
But the taboo surrounding the Palestinian issue seems to apply to everyone,
especially those in the art world.” She sees this edge of control and
containment of creative expression as the stark reality of the role that
culture plays in the United States: “Faced with silence, self-censorship, and
the ‘public execution’ of artistic careers, I believe those of us working in
the cultural sphere are confronting a terrifying reality: the decline of
culture's power. Now, more than ever, we need to see a surge of artworks that
actively challenge this situation.”

**Your work contains a mind-boggling array of references to nuclear history
and military science. How did you first become interested in the nuclear
issue?**

My interest in nuclear issues began in 2016, when my father, a former civil
engineer, was called to supervise the restoration of a major road near the
Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant. Five years had passed since the
devastating meltdowns, fear and anxiety, and I was shocked to realize how
little I cared about the current situation in Fukushima. I realized the fear
of forgetting the fear. As I researched the issue out of concern for my
father's health, I realized how unreliable the mass media and government
information was, and how much would remain hidden if we didn't investigate
ourselves. This marked the beginning of my research-based work, mindful of the
invisibility, both physical and political, of radiation and the nuclear
industry. At the time, I was a first-year student in the MFA program at SUNY
Purchase College and the campus was in constant turmoil because of the first
inauguration of the Trump administration, While my classmates and professors
were in lively discussions about politics and anxiety, I was worrying about
Fukushima.

I usually start to research historical archives, especially photographs, then
visit the locations, including military and nuclear facilities and former
sites. This was significant to me, as I hadn’t really seen these facilities in
my life. I also visit museums to confirm the "official" narratives. The most
exciting research is meeting and interviewing survivors to uncover untold
stories. I encountered their unique words describing their extreme
experiences, which made me want to draw. Also, I got advice from [Robert
Jacobs](https://bojacobs.net/), the historian of nuclear technologies, and
other experts so as not to miss the newest aspect and analysis to discuss.

Regarding Palestine, I began speaking with individuals and families in Gaza
and Egypt via DM. I noted their words about harsh condition. Most were
students and told their dreams. They sent me photos of destroyed house and
sounds of bombings and drones. A Palestinian-American activist I met at a
protest became a significant figure to me; he embodied the very "reality of
the Palestinian issue" that transcends national borders. Interviewing a
Japanese journalist who has visited Palestine more than 70 times helped me to
analyze the ongoing situation. The most influential book for me was
[_Necropolitics_ by Achille Mbembe](https://www.dukeupress.edu/necropolitics).
I had read it to understand the nuclear colonial issue, and later I noticed
that Mbembe wrote a lot about Palestine.

Before I become overwhelmed by the immense volume of information, I encourage
myself to move my hands and eyes—working on paper, canvas, or wood. Even after
much research, many things remain unclear until I actually attempt to build
with the materials. And when I draw, my vision becomes much more acute. It
compels me to gaze intently at—and imagine—those vague, nebulous areas and
regions of indistinct outline, urging me to comprehend what is unfolding
within them. In the process, I seek unexpected ideas that transform the work
and the direction of my next research. Through this practice, I engage with
information and the world in a manner entirely unique to me.

I constantly investigate how storytelling—films, manga, novels, poetry,
art—depicts nuclear weapons and war. I have developed my perspectives and
ideas as an artist between growing up in post-war Tokyo and living in the U.S.
I have a simple doubt: many manga and films I adored depict a world ravaged by
radiation, post-World War III, and interstellar warfare. So why do Japanese
tend to be indifferent to the realities of actual war and nuclear issues,
including me? Pop culture plays a pivotal role as propaganda in imperialism,
like how Hollywood has been working with the government since WWII. Critical
inquiry into culture and how our collective consciousness has been shaped by
it is a significant layer of my work.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-4-scaled.jpeg)

_Window_ , 2024. Sumi ink on paper, 14 x 11 inches (35.6 x 27.9 cm). Private
Collection. © Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Ulterior Gallery, New York

**As a Japanese artist living in New York for the past 20 years, do you see a
difference between how your art is received in Japan versus in the United
States? Are there themes or ideas in your work that a Japanese audience is
willing to address but an American audience isn’t — and vice versa?**

For my work—which depicts political themes—the differences between Japan and
the U.S. are inextricably linked to the relationship between art and society.
I create multiple "entry points" to engage a broad spectrum of viewers. Some
Japanese people are not familiar with contemporary art. In Japan, manga and
anime are far more effective as media for raising conversation and collective
consciousness; this reality in my home country is a significant element of my
hybrid artistic forms. I don’t simplify my expression to cater to the masses;
I try to create work that subverts expectations, provokes astonishment, and
stimulates the imagination.

My use of animal characters—intended to transcend the category of nationality
and race—and the inclusion of global _Hibakusha_ , were for both American and
Japanese viewers. In Japan, there is a tendency to question the legitimacy of
anyone speaking about the atomic bombings if they do not hail from the
affected regions. Both the government and the people create a deliberate
distance to avoid confronting the reality of the bombings. An artist friend
from Hiroshima encouraged me, "Unless people outside of Hiroshima also speak
up, it is difficult to change." These are words I have cherished ever since.
My work seeks to carve out new breakthroughs for connecting with "others," and
sometimes, those "others" are Japanese.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-5-scaled.jpeg)

_First Class_ , 2024. Sumi ink on paper, 14 x 11 inches (35.6 x 27.9 cm).
Private Collection © Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Ulterior Gallery, New York

In contrast, in the U.S., contemporary art is the strongest genre and wields
immense influence on people and society. Consequently, there has been an
abundance of politically charged artwork. I also believe that if a work is
well-crafted and persuasive, my work with a controversial theme could find its
way.

In 2020, I received a commission from the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center at
the University of Texas at El Paso. [_ENOLA 'S
HEAD_](https://web.archive.org/web/20211022131532/https://www.utep.edu/rubin/exhibitions/current/gaku-
tsutaja-enolas-head.html) is a project centered on a life-sized replica of the
Enola Gay's nose cone, made of metal, wood, and fabric, transformed into a
theater for a 56-min animation video. The video consists of 47 drawings,
sculptures, and performances with 14 protagonist masks about nuclear history.
The masks were made using the Gigaku mask technique. Gigaku is an ancient
masked theater performance form whose hybrid nature reached Japan via the Silk
Road and eventually fell out of practice 14,000 years ago. By drawing upon
this cultural heritage, which, despite once vanishing, has been preserved into
the modern era, I have crafted a narrative set in a "future" in which humanity
has already gone extinct. Through a critical examination of the fact that
rival nations have historically concealed the true extent of radiation damage,
the work explores the underlying causes of the human race's extinction. With
nonhuman protagonists, this work seeks to reveal that war is not merely a
conflict between nations, but rather a struggle between the state and its
citizens, or between capital and the people; in doing so, it challenges and
rewrites the "narrative of victory" symbolized by the Enola Gay. I received
great responses at the Rubin Center and the [2022 Hawaiʻi
Triennale](https://hawaiicontemporary.org/artist-gaku-tsutaja), both locations
with large military bases. A week later, Russia launched a full-scale invasion
of Ukraine and the curator featured my work as an anti-war symbol. ENOLA’S
HEAD was supposed to travel to [Maruki
Gallery](https://marukigallery.jp/event-en/220723/) after the Hawaiʻi
Triennale. But because the Ukraine war started, shipping was delayed and I had
to make a last-minute change for the installation. It was the first time that
war had directly prevented my exhibition.

But over the past two years, as I began incorporating elements related to
Palestine and Israel, different tensions have arisen in response to my anti-
war works.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-6-scaled.jpeg)

_ENOLA’S HEAD_ , 2021-22 Linen fabric, blackout fabric, wood, electric
conduit, plastic, vintage lump shade, vintage bomber seat belts, vintage
protected hood, vintage backpack, vintage canteen, glass bottles, bamboo,
legless seat backs, turtle shell, Elk’s horns, wood powder, wheat flour, wood
glue, hemp cloth, paper clay, projector, amplifier, speakers, video 9′ 6″ x
24’ 5″ x 10′ 9 5/8″ (This work is installed 12” above the floor） Photo by
Edgar Picazo Merino. ©Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Stanlee & Gerald Rubin Center
for the Visual Arts at University of Texas at El Paso, and Ulterior Gallery,
New York

**You have been publicly vocal about the genocide in Gaza and have included
references to Palestine in your most recent sculptural works, specifically a
cardboard sign painted with the word “Rafah” — the southernmost city in Gaza
at the border with Egypt that has been completely obliterated by the Israeli
military. How has your support for Palestine been received in the art world?**

I usually create fictional names for nations or places, keeping the
nonfictional name for projects or weapons. But "Rafah" was part of my sign
which I had used at protests. It was one of the rain-soaked, tattered protest
signs I'd peeled off and scattered as part of the sculpture. There's also a
torn-off poster of Netanyahu's face hanging from a branch, a souvenir from my
Palestinian American friend. This sculpture is a strategic diorama in which
imaginary monk parakeets simulate exterminating the giant spider that has
taken up residence in the human brain. Incorporating real-world actions or
elements into my fictional narrative is one of my favorite methods. I always
want to challenge the border between different layers to shake the stable
territories. At the opening, I spoke with many people who were passionate
about the issues, but I saw some clouded expressions and heard later,
indirectly, that someone felt that my political statements ruined the work.
These ranges of reaction reflect the state of our division. I let my work
talk, but as I am not an observer, it is natural for me to engage the audience
in conversations through the work. And "Rafah," situated within an acceptable
theatrical space teeming with animals, insects, allegories, and symbols,
served as an element that could remind us of a parallel world, our reality.

In the art, film, or music industries, we have a surprising level of silence
for political statements, consciously or unconsciously, surrounding Israel.
What kind of situation is it when we CAN express in our art form about the
genocidal civilization that has had such a profound impact on our emotions,
thinking, human rights, and economy, but better NOT to do it in political
words?Express yourself through art—but keep your mouth shut? Is there a
territory where artists must stay?

When someone tells me I shouldn’t talk about it, it just shows our society is
imprisoning our souls right now. My political statements should not damage my
work. My words simply came out as I shouldered the weight of creation: its
motivation, its journey, and its current reality of continuous crimes against
humanity.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/76D6D6D1-74E3-4CCA-8103-F42C89EE28EC-680x453.jpeg)

Details of Pidgingo-no-Inko: Project Head, 2025. © Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of
Ulterior Gallery, New York



![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-7.jpeg)

_Pidgingo-no-Inko: Project Head_ , 2025. Mixed media, video 20 min. 7 feet x 7
feet x 4 feet and 2 inches. © Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Ulterior Gallery, New
York

**Do you consider yourself an anti-war or anti-nuclear activist?**

I call myself an artist and hesitate to call myself an activist. But meeting
and following activists’ actions is significant for me as an artist because
the responsibility of being an artist lies in questioning existing power
structures and dismantling the rituals that reinforce them. Since learning
about the concealment of nuclear disasters, my interest has been if or how we
can really stop the wars. I cannot portray the structural nature of war and
its potential dismantling without understanding activism.

My first anti-nuclear and anti-war activists were _Hibakusha_. I was
profoundly influenced by a second-generation _Hibakusha_ in Hiroshima who is a
lifelong activist. She taught me so much about the backstory of Japanese anti-
war activism history. In the U.S., I have met with and listened to the stories
of various activists: a Spokane tribal activist leader and former uranium
miner; the director of "Hanford Challenge," a watchdog organization monitoring
the Hanford Site; a former worker and a downwinder of the Hanford Site; and a
Marshallese activist from Bikini Atoll. In the process of transforming their
stories into artistic form, considering their heavy experiences and legacies,
my work and soul have been tempered and strengthened.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-8-scaled.jpeg)

_Memory Bug: Peace Memorial Day_ , 2023 Sumi ink and gesso on wood panel 33
3/4 x 25 7/8 x 1 5/8 in (85.7 x 65.7 x 4.1 cm) © Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of
Ulterior Gallery, New York

**As an artist whose work overtly addresses issues of militarization, nuclear
weapons, and endless imperial wars, do you ever find it challenging to be in
your studio? What keeps you coming back to making artwork despite the
terrifying scenarios of war that we are witnessing daily?**

I often feel impatient. I want to share my ideas as quickly as possible. But
we are currently confronted with a stark reality: despite the countless
historical expressions and social movements that have emerged to challenge
issues such as state power and the military-industrial complex, the world
continues to be drawn inexorably toward ill. For this reason—while
acknowledging that activism is essential as a "frontline" of resistance—I need
to think and take action about what art and culture have done for this world.
Since I began engaging with nuclear issues, I have been preoccupied with the
relationship between war and culture. When I encounter well-twisted
propaganda, I feel so shocked. The crisis in Palestine has exposed a
regrettable truth: it is not only Hollywood but the art world—a realm that
ought to be a bastion of the avant-garde—that plays a role in this dynamic.

Japanese manga and anime industry has helped "normalize" nuclear weapons and
wars; in response, I created a series titled _Memory Bug_. Since 2023, I have
been conducting research into the manipulation of consciousness through
American culture. My work _Pidgingo-no-Inko_ features scenes exploring various
themes: the pitfalls of anti-imperialist critique found in H.G. Wells’s “The
War of the Worlds”; the "double propaganda" embedded in the jazz music and
radio programs—such as “This is the Truth”—broadcast during the American
occupation of Japan; and the controversy surrounding the producer of
“Oppenheimer” for having disseminated the hashtag #killthemall.

Culture has, in capitalism, transformed into a formidable weapon—one that
constructs collective consciousness by mass-producing and disseminating
narratives that serve to uphold and reinforce imperialism.

Our reality currently stands in a critical state, imperiled by the military-
industrial complex and nuclear weapons. At this very moment, Iran has been
attacked and is fighting back against the U.S. and Israel, continuing bombing
and starving Palestinians, and the crackdown on immigrants and activists
within the U.S. itself has intensified. AI is escalating the speed of
production, propaganda, surveillance, targeting systems, and the energy war
increasing nuclear power, pollution, and water consumption—at every level it
has infiltrated our daily lives. The world is teetering on the brink of
collapse, accelerating at a terrifying pace. My central theme has always been
'transformation,' and right now, I feel a profound need for it.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-9.jpeg)

_Conqueror Hat_ , 2025 Sumi ink, Gouache, and color pencil on paper 22 5/8 x
30 1/8 inches (57.5 x 76.5 cm) © Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Ulterior Gallery,
New York

**How have you been inspired by the global movement for Palestinian
Liberation?**

I felt hope that perhaps, this time, state violence might finally be brought
to an end by the international solidarity movement for Palestinian liberation.
In New York, anti-Zionist Jewish groups were strong and clearly articulated
the distinction between Zionism and Judaism, which the mass media tried to
trap us in. In front of the Atomic Bomb Dome in Hiroshima, Rebecca, you raised
your voice with unwavering conviction; the social media posts by the Hiroshima
group have encouraged me so much. I was truly happy that I was able to
participate there.

In my work _Pidgingo-no-Inko_ , by montaging images from various eras and
locations, I aimed to express how the overlapping histories of oppression
forge an unshakable bond of solidarity. On social media, I received backlash
from Asian users because of my comments connecting the tragedy for _Hibakusha_
and Palestinians. When I talked with American friends in person, I naturally
mentioned the history of Imperial Japan and its postwar complicity with
American diplomacy, and their faces lit up, and their eyes met mine. But
still, I often felt I stuck out.

The stronger our solidarity, the stronger the collusion between capital, state
power, mass media, and online manipulation. It has not been easy to bridge the
divides between people close to me over historical perceptions and political
participation. Of paramount importance to me was to depict these recurring
situations—to portray the fact that the seeds of war could lie within
ourselves.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-10.jpeg)

The author & Gaku Tsutaja at the Hiroshima Atomic Bomb Dome, June 2025. Photo
by Nakaoku Takeo.

At the family party on Christmas, I couldn’t stop talking about the genocide
after they asked me, “How are you?” As my brain was full of thoughts and work,
my machine-gun talk destroyed the atmosphere. Later, I drew a satire of this
scene, portraying myself in a kamikaze pilot uniform. I am living in the
empire again. What stirred my complexity of emotions even more than the fear
of state surveillance has been the divergence of opinions and levels of
concern among the people closest to me. It engendered a sense of isolation and
fear.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-11-scaled.jpeg)

_Holiday_ , 2024, Sumi ink and acrylic on paper 14×11 inches (35.6 x 27.9 cm).
©Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Ulterior Gallery, New York

Silence will only help the oppressor and destroy us in the end. But still, the
brain has a way of ignoring and forgetting to maintain our “peace.” The
oppressor uses it. In the world of capitalism, genocide, stealing, and
imprisonment have always been a parallel world of our “democracy.” They killed
so many journalists in Gaza because they haven’t given up on reporting what is
going on. When violence escalates to divide us, resistance must escalate to
connect as well. Since the State and Capital have always executed their
violence with meticulous preparation and vision, those on the side of
resistance must prepare ourselves to stand with our visions. Historically and
right now, they have accumulated techniques and strategies of mass murder.
Breaking through the divisions among people requires trial and error; the
direct actions, such as the physical dismantling of weapons factories were
remarkable acts. Activists are taking action at great personal risk, and have
been killed by the IOF, ICE, state troopers, Border Patrol agents. The anti-
nuclear activists whom I interviewed continued their activism for their
communities despite battling Parkinson’s disease and cancers; three of them
passed away. They were killed by governments that had concealed the true
reality of radiation exposure. When I interviewed them, I felt that the
stories of their lives with deformed children, sheep born with extra legs, and
threats from the government were even more harrowing than any sci-fi dystopia.
And I have seen the similar level situation in Gaza in real time. There is a
report of a cluster of rare cancers around the AI data center. All survivors
are still in hell. Witnessing so many deaths, the eyes, minds, and hearts of
those who still care have been damaged. The current situation has escalated to
the point of disrupting the daily lives of the majority of people, but still,
we cannot stop this madness.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-416696-12.jpeg)

_Daily Drawings: Spider’s Thread Day 36, Classified Specimens_ , 2020, Sumi
ink and acrylic on paper 14×11 inches (35.6 x 27.9 cm). Private Collection
©Gaku Tsutaja; Courtesy of Ulterior Gallery, New York

In this "civilization" that has long harbored genocide deep within its
structure and is now laying bare its true nature, artists also should face it
and work desperately harder on the creation and development of a unique
language that can dismantle our own existence as one held captive by the
system and can take us to the outside. Artists play a role as a countermeasure
against desolation and against the normalization of our condition, of silence,
and of the casting aside of "parallel worlds" as a way to survive. "Surviving"
and "living" are two distinct things. Alongside those who strive to bring
about the ethical evolution, shifting between despair and hope in this
transforming era, I will continue to dig tunnels yet unknown and question.

_Pidgingo-no-Inko_ ends with the line narrated by~~~~ the protagonist, who was
arrested for burning the flag of the Nation of Ikai: “Who is really in the
cage?”

Gaku Tsutaja’s work can be found at
[gakutsutaja.net](https://www.gakutsutaja.net/) or on Instagram at
@monkparakeets
